lede: Every formula is a story about one letter. Making $x$ the subject means rewriting it so that letter sits alone on one side and everything else on the other. Here the subject can be squared, under a root, inside a fraction, or — the case that empties the most marks — in two places at once.
can: Undo the operations in reverse order, keeping the equation balanced.
Gather a subject that appears twice, then factorise it out.
Clear a denominator or a power before anything else.

text: Changing the subject when the easy method runs out

md: Read a formula as a machine acting on the subject, and rearranging becomes unwrapping. In $y = \sqrt{3x+5}$ the machine multiplies by 3, adds 5, then square-roots; to get $x$ back you undo those three in reverse. Whatever you do to one side you do to the other, so the equation stays balanced the whole way.

prompt: In the formula $y = 5x - 8$, which letter is the subject at the moment?
answer: y | Y | the y | y is
explain: $y$. It sits alone on one side and appears nowhere else. Making $x$ the subject means handing that job over to $x$.

title: The statement
md:
**M7-NA-07** — change the subject of a formula, including cases where a power or root of the subject appears and cases where the subject appears in more than one term.
The Teacher Guidance names the two formulae it has in mind: $A = \pi r^2$ and $P = \dfrac{100(s-c)}{c}$. Both of them are waiting for you further down this page.
source: CCEA GCSE Mathematics specification, statement M7-NA-07 and its Teacher Guidance

prompt: The statement names two harder cases. Which of these is **not** one of them?
options: A rearrangement that needs the quadratic formula
A power or a root of the subject
The subject appearing in more than one term
answer: A rearrangement that needs the quadratic formula
explain: Powers, roots and a repeated subject are all on the statement. A formula that turns into a quadratic in the subject is not, and no CCEA paper read for this page set one, so if your working produces $x^2$ and $x$ together you have taken a wrong turning.

text: The balance, and the locked box

md:
Two pictures carry this whole topic.
**The balance.** An equals sign is a pair of scales sitting level. Take 4 off one pan and you must take 4 off the other, or it tips. The same goes for multiplying, dividing, squaring and rooting: **whatever you do, do it to the whole of both sides**. That is the only rule in the topic; everything else is a choice about what to do next.

prompt: An equals sign says the two sides weigh the same. What keeps them equal?
options: Doing the same thing to both sides
Doing the opposite thing to each side
answer: Doing the same thing to both sides
explain: Anything done to one side has to be done to the other, or the two sides stop balancing.

md: **The locked box.** The subject has been wrapped up — multiplied, then added to, then rooted. To get it out you unwrap in the **opposite order**: the last thing on is the first thing off, the same reason your coat comes off before your jumper.

prompt: The scales balance at $3x + 4 = 19$. You take 4 off both pans. What is now on the right-hand pan?
explain: $19 - 4 = 15$, and the left pan is down to $3x$. Divide each pan by 3 and $x = 5$.

md:
Read the formula as a machine acting on the subject. In $y = \sqrt{3x+5}$ the machine does three things to $x$: multiply by 3, add 5, take the square root. To make $x$ the subject you run the machine backwards from $y$: square, subtract 5, divide by 3. That gives $x = \dfrac{y^2 - 5}{3}$.
Writing the chain out line by line is not showing off. Each link of the reverse chain is one line of your working, and CCEA pays for those lines: in summer 2023 a mark was sitting on the intermediate line alone, before anybody had finished the question.

prompt: In $y = \sqrt{3x+5}$, which operation do you undo first?
explain: It was the last thing done to $x$, so it is the first thing off. Square both sides and you are left with $y^2 = 3x + 5$.

prompt: Temperatures convert by $F = \dfrac{9C}{5} + 32$. Make $C$ the subject, then work out $C$ when $F = 68$.
explain: Backwards: subtract 32, multiply by 5, divide by 9, so $C = \dfrac{5(F-32)}{9}$. With $F = 68$ that is $\dfrac{5 \times 36}{9} = 20$.

text: See it once, then do it

md: One video, then straight back to work. Watch it through once for the shape of the method rather than for the numbers, and answer the question underneath from memory.

title: Changing the Subject Advanced
why: Corbettmaths video 8 takes the harder cases in the same order as this lesson: powers and roots first, then the subject appearing twice.

prompt: The subject appears in two separate terms. Which order of moves finishes the job?
options: Collect the subject terms, factorise the subject out, divide by the bracket
Divide by the subject, then collect what is left
Factorise first, then collect the subject terms
answer: Collect the subject terms, factorise the subject out, divide by the bracket
explain: Dividing by the subject leaves a copy of it behind, and there is nothing to factorise until the terms are side by side. Collect, factorise, divide, in that order.

md: A square is undone by a square root and a root by a square — but only once the power is standing on its own. In $B = Ar^2 + 5$ the $r^2$ has been multiplied by $A$ and had 5 added to it, so subtract 5, then divide by $A$, and only then root: $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{B-5}{A}}$. Rooting early gives $\dfrac{\sqrt{B-5}}{A}$, which is a different number for almost every $A$.

prompt: $m = \sqrt{n+7}$, and $n$ is to be the subject. Which is right?
explain: Square both sides first: $m^2 = n + 7$. Then subtract 7. The second answer adds 7 the wrong way; the third halves $m$ instead of squaring it.

md: Two more habits. The root sign covers **the whole of that side**, not the numerator only. And a square root has two values: write $\pm$ unless the letter is a length, a radius, a time or a speed, in which case say in one clause why you dropped the negative.

prompt: $B = Ar^2 + 5$, and $r$ is a radius. Which is the finished answer?
explain: Subtract 5, divide by $A$, then root the whole of what is left. The second answer roots before dividing; the third halves the square instead of rooting it. A radius is positive, so the negative root is dropped and you say so.

text: When the subject turns up twice

md: This is the case examiners write about every single year. If $x$ sits in two terms you cannot divide your way out, because dividing by $x$ leaves another $x$ behind. Three moves, always in this order:

prompt: Three marks, the subject appears twice, and you have run out of time after collecting the terms. Name the one line that would earn the next mark.
answer: the factorised line | factorise | the factorised form | factorising | x(...) = ... | take x out of a bracket | factorise out x | the bracket line
explain: The factorised line, with the subject outside a single bracket. It is the middle of the three marks, and it makes the final division obvious.

md:
**1 Collect** — every term containing $x$ onto one side, everything else onto the other.
**2 Factorise** — take $x$ outside a bracket so it appears exactly once.
**3 Divide** — by the whole bracket, not by one term of it.
For $8x - 3w = wx + 12$: collecting gives $8x - wx = 12 + 3w$, factorising gives $x(8-w) = 12 + 3w$, dividing gives $x = \dfrac{12+3w}{8-w}$. Three lines, and the CCEA scheme pays a mark for each one.

prompt: $5t = ht + 9$, and $t$ is to be the subject. What is the first line you write?
explain: Both $t$ terms move to the same side first. The second option moves the wrong term and leaves $t$ on both sides; the third divides while $t$ is still on the right, so nothing has been made the subject.

prompt: Finish the factorised line for $5t - ht = 9$. Write it as $t(\ldots) = 9$ — what goes inside the bracket?
explain: $t(5-h) = 9$. Each term gave up its $t$, leaving 5 and $-h$ inside the bracket. Dividing by that whole bracket gives $t = \dfrac{9}{5-h}$.

md: A fraction is a division waiting to be undone, so undo it before anything else: multiply **every term on both sides** by the denominator. In $k = \dfrac{2n}{n+5}$, multiplying both sides by $(n+5)$ gives $k(n+5) = 2n$, which expands to $kn + 5k = 2n$. The subject is now in two terms, so you are straight back to collect, factorise, divide: $5k = 2n - kn$, then $5k = n(2-k)$, then $n = \dfrac{5k}{2-k}$.

prompt: $y = \dfrac{3w+1}{5}$, and $w$ is to be the subject. What is the first move?
explain: The whole of $3w+1$ is being divided by 5, so undo the division first: $5y = 3w + 1$. Only then subtract 1 and divide by 3, giving $w = \dfrac{5y-1}{3}$.

text: Two minutes that save three marks

md:
Rearranging is the one topic that marks itself. Choose an easy value for each of the other letters, work your subject out from **your** answer, then put every value back into the **original** formula and see whether the two sides agree.
Take $n = \dfrac{5k}{2-k}$ and try $k = 1.5$: then $n = \dfrac{7.5}{0.5} = 15$. Back into the original formula: $\dfrac{2 \times 15}{15+5} = \dfrac{30}{20} = 1.5$, which is the $k$ you started with. If the two sides disagree you have caught a sign slip while there is still time to fix it.

prompt: Check $x = \dfrac{12+3w}{8-w}$ against $8x - 3w = wx + 12$ by putting $w = 2$ in. What value of $x$ do you get from your answer?
explain: $\dfrac{12+6}{8-2} = \dfrac{18}{6} = 3$. Now check: $8(3) - 3(2) = 18$ and $2(3) + 12 = 18$, so the two sides agree and the rearrangement is sound.

text: Where the marks are actually lost

title: Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q6
md: Three marks for one rearrangement with the subject in two terms, and under half of the entry took all three. Over a third never gathered the subject terms onto one side, which is the move the first mark is for. Underline both terms containing the subject before you write anything.

prompt: You reach $9x - cx = 4 + c$ and the clock is running out. What is the best use of the next ten seconds?
options: Cross it out and start again
explain: That single line is worth a mark on its own and it hands you the last step as well: divide by the bracket to get $x = \dfrac{4+c}{9-c}$. Dividing by 9 alone leaves the $cx$ untouched.

title: Why the subject has to be gathered first
md: A letter on both sides is two jobs at once. Bringing both of its terms to the same side lets you write the subject once, as a single factor, and only then can it be divided out. That is why the first mark is for the gathering and the next for the bracket.

prompt: Rearranging $p - 5n = q$ for $n$, write the intermediate line that gets the $5n$ on its own. Fill in: $p - q = \ldots$
explain: $p - q = 5n$. That line alone carries a mark. Dividing by 5 then gives $n = \dfrac{p-q}{5}$; watch the sign, because $-5n$ becomes $+5n$ when it crosses the equals sign.

title: Sheet or memory?
md:
**On the M7 and M8 formula sheet (page 2):** nothing for this topic. It carries the prism, trapezium, sphere and cone formulae, the quadratic formula and the trigonometric rules — so a question may hand you a cone or a sphere formula and then ask you to rearrange it, but never the rearranging itself.
**Must be known:** do the same thing to the whole of both sides; undo operations in reverse order; collect, factorise, divide when the subject appears twice; a square root covers the whole side and has two values unless the context rules one out; $A = \pi r^2$ gives $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$.

prompt: Which of these is printed on page 2 of the M7 paper?
options: The rule for making a squared letter the subject
explain: The sheet carries mensuration, the quadratic formula and the trigonometric rules. The area of a circle and every rearranging rule have to be known, which is why the cone formula gets set as a rearranging question.

md:
Undo the operations in reverse order, both sides together.
Gather a repeated subject on one side and factorise it out.
Clear fractions and powers before anything else.
Check by substituting easy numbers.

Expect a single part worth 2 or 3 marks, usually in the second half of either paper, and the same rearrangement often set on M7 and M8 in one series. The first mark is for the gathering or the first clean undoing; the last is the subject alone, with the sign checked. Stuck: write the intermediate line anyway, because a mark is usually there for it.
